claim: STORM resolved two distinct layers of agrinC within the GBM.
source: In contrast to conventional immunofluorescence images of agrin, STORM resolved two distinct layers of agrinC within the GBM (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 1A,B demonstrating two distinct layers of agrinC

claim: The gap between agrinC layers showed a mean peak-to-peak distance of 137.9 nm ± 1.9 nm SEM for 80 regions.
source: The gap between agrinC layers, measured as the peak-to-peak distance, showed a mean of 137.9 nm ± 1.9 nm standard error of mean (SEM) for the 80 regions; the distance was 132.7 nm (±0.9 nm) across more than 600 GBM regions (Figure 1D).
evidence: Quantitative measurements from 80 regions analyzed by STORM

claim: The distance between agrinC layers was 132.7 nm (±0.9 nm) across more than 600 GBM regions.
source: The gap between agrinC layers, measured as the peak-to-peak distance, showed a mean of 137.9 nm ± 1.9 nm standard error of mean (SEM) for the 80 regions; the distance was 132.7 nm (±0.9 nm) across more than 600 GBM regions (Figure 1D).
evidence: Quantitative measurements from more than 600 GBM regions analyzed by STORM

claim: The two layers of agrinC were localized between two layers of podocalyxin.
source: Dual channel STORM imaging showed that the two layers of agrinC were indeed localized between two layers of podocalyxin (Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Dual channel STORM imaging data showing spatial relationship between agrinC and podocalyxin

claim: Podocalyxin labeled endothelial cells as well as podocytes.
source: Superimposition of the podocalyxin-agrinC STORM image with deep-etch EM confirmed that podocalyxin labeled endothelial cells as well as podocytes, while agrin was localized to the GBM (Figure 1H).
evidence: STORM-EM correlation showing podocalyxin localization to both cell types

claim: Agrin was localized to the GBM.
source: Superimposition of the podocalyxin-agrinC STORM image with deep-etch EM confirmed that podocalyxin labeled endothelial cells as well as podocytes, while agrin was localized to the GBM (Figure 1H).
evidence: STORM-EM correlation confirming agrin localization

claim: AgrinN was present in two layers that were shifted slightly internally to the two agrinC layers, with center positions at −57.5 ± 2.8 nm and 50.2 ± 3.28 nm.
source: In contrast, co-labeling with antibodies to agrinN and agrinC showed that agrinN was present in two layers that were shifted slightly internally to the two agrinC layers, with center positions at −57.5 ± 2.8 nm and 50.2 ± 3.28 nm (Figure 2A).
evidence: Quantitative STORM data from co-labeling experiments measuring positions of agrinN relative to agrinC

claim: Agrin is oriented either perpendicular or oblique to the plane of the GBM with the C-terminus nearest the adjacent cells, and the N-terminus closer to the center of the GBM.
source: This suggests that agrin is oriented either perpendicular or oblique to the plane of the GBM with the C-terminus nearest the adjacent cells, and the N-terminus, which binds the coiled-coil domain of laminin γ1, closer to the center of the GBM.
evidence: Inference from the differential positioning of agrinN and agrinC measured by STORM

claim: The agrin N-terminus binds the coiled-coil domain of laminin γ1.
source: This suggests that agrin is oriented either perpendicular or oblique to the plane of the GBM with the C-terminus nearest the adjacent cells, and the N-terminus, which binds the coiled-coil domain of laminin γ1, closer to the center of the GBM.
evidence: Referenced from established biochemical knowledge about agrin-laminin interactions

claim: The orientation and mapping of agrinC and agrinN to different locations within the GBM is consistent with the distinct molecular interactions of the two agrin domains.
source: The orientation and mapping of agrinC and agrinN to different locations within the GBM is consistent with the distinct molecular interactions of the two agrin domains as well as the ∼95 nm extended conformation of agrin visualized by EM (Denzer et al., 1998).
evidence: Comparison of STORM data with known biochemical interactions and EM structural data from literature

claim: Agrin has a ∼95 nm extended conformation as visualized by EM.
source: The orientation and mapping of agrinC and agrinN to different locations within the GBM is consistent with the distinct molecular interactions of the two agrin domains as well as the ∼95 nm extended conformation of agrin visualized by EM (Denzer et al., 1998).
evidence: Cited from previous EM study by Denzer et al., 1998

claim: Integrin β1 showed two layers with center positions at -79.6 ± 3.3 nm towards the endothelial side and 77.1 ± 3.4 nm towards the podocyte side.
source: The center positions of each integrin layer were calculated at -79.6 ± 3.3 nm towards the endothelial side and 77.1 ± 3.4 nm towards the podocyte side.
evidence: Quantitative STORM measurements of integrin β1 positions

claim: Integrin β1 distribution closely overlaps with agrinC, with a slight outward shift towards the cell membranes.
source: The histograms as well as the center positions of integrin β1 indicate a distribution that closely overlaps with agrinC, with a slight outward shift towards the cell membranes.
evidence: Comparison of STORM localization histograms and center positions for integrin β1 and agrinC

claim: LMβ2-LF localized between the agrinC layers at −3.2 ± 2.5 nm.
source: Co-labeling with anti-agrinC showed that LMβ2-LF localized between the agrinC layers at −3.2 ± 2.5 nm (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantitative STORM measurements from co-labeling experiments

claim: The position of LMα5-LEb/L4b mapped in the middle of the GBM, at −1.8 ± 3.6 nm.
source: Similar to LMβ2-LF, the position of LMα5-LEb/L4b also mapped in the middle of the GBM, at −1.8 ± 3.6 nm (Figure 2D).
evidence: Quantitative STORM measurements of LMα5-LEb/L4b position

claim: The span between the N- and C-termini of laminin α5 forms the long 'vertical' axis of the LM-521 cruciform trimer and is estimated to be 130 to 150 nm.
source: The span between the N- and C-termini of laminin α5 forms the long 'vertical' axis of the LM-521 cruciform trimer. Based on data from electron micrographs and crystal structures of various laminin domains, this axis is estimated to be 130 to 150 nm, while the horizontal axis, composed of the β2 and γ1 short arms, spans 70 to 80 nm (Beck et al., 1990; Yurchenco and Cheng, 1993; Sasaki et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from previous structural studies using EM and crystallography

claim: The horizontal axis of LM-521, composed of the β2 and γ1 short arms, spans 70 to 80 nm.
source: The span between the N- and C-termini of laminin α5 forms the long 'vertical' axis of the LM-521 cruciform trimer. Based on data from electron micrographs and crystal structures of various laminin domains, this axis is estimated to be 130 to 150 nm, while the horizontal axis, composed of the β2 and γ1 short arms, spans 70 to 80 nm (Beck et al., 1990; Yurchenco and Cheng, 1993; Sasaki et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from previous structural studies

claim: The positions of the LMα5-LG domain were calculated at 88.3 ± 3.07 nm towards the podocyte side and −84.7 ± 6.7 nm towards the endothelial side.
source: The positions of the LMα5-LG domain were calculated at 88.3 ± 3.07 nm towards the podocyte side and −84.7 ± 6.7 nm towards the endothelial side.
evidence: Quantitative STORM measurements from transgenic mice expressing human laminin α5

claim: LM-521 trimers are oriented with their C-terminal LG domains near the outer aspects of the GBM and their N-terminal domains towards the center of the GBM.
source: Together with the data for LMα5-LEb/L4b (Figure 2D), this shows that LM-521 trimers are oriented with their C-terminal LG domains near the outer aspects of the GBM and their N-terminal domains towards the center of the GBM.
evidence: Inference from combined STORM measurements of multiple laminin domains

claim: The GBM's laminin component is divided into two networks, one produced by podocytes and the other by endothelial cells.
source: The most straightforward interpretation is that the GBM's laminin component is divided into two networks, one produced by podocytes and the other by endothelial cells.
evidence: Inference from STORM data showing cell-specific laminin localization in transgenic mice

claim: The two laminin networks either overlap or are so close to each other that they are indistinguishable by STORM.
source: The single band seen with the N-terminal antibody in the center of the GBM occurred because the two networks either overlap or are so close to each other that they are indistinguishable by STORM.
evidence: Inference from STORM imaging showing single band for N-terminal laminin despite two separate networks

claim: There is limited mobility of laminin trimers across the thickness of the GBM.
source: In the vast majority of glomeruli, we observed that neither podocyte- nor endothelium-derived LM-521 crossed/flipped over, demonstrating that there is limited mobility of laminin trimers across the thickness of the GBM.
evidence: Observation from STORM imaging of cell-specific laminin expression in transgenic mice

claim: A similar conclusion about limited laminin mobility was reported for the endogenous laminin trimer using a different method.
source: A similar conclusion was also reported for the endogenous laminin trimer using a different method (Abrahamson et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous study by Abrahamson et al., 2007

claim: Collagen IV chains contain a long collagenous domain composed of interrupted Gly-X-Y amino acid triplet repeats situated between non-collagenous N-terminal (7S) and C-terminal (NC1) domains.
source: Collagen IV chains contain a long collagenous domain composed of interrupted Gly-X-Y amino acid triplet repeats situated between non-collagenous N-terminal (7S) and C-terminal (NC1) domains (Hudson et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about collagen IV structure

claim: Collagen IV chains assemble intracellularly into ∼400 nm long triple helical heterotrimers that are secreted into the ECM.
source: These chains assemble intracellularly into ∼400 nm long triple helical heterotrimers (also known as protomers) that are secreted into the ECM, where they polymerize via hexameric NC1 and dodecameric 7S interactions to form a chicken wire-like network one to several chains thick (Khoshnoodi et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about collagen IV assembly

claim: Collagen IV protomers polymerize via hexameric NC1 and dodecameric 7S interactions to form a chicken wire-like network.
source: These chains assemble intracellularly into ∼400 nm long triple helical heterotrimers (also known as protomers) that are secreted into the ECM, where they polymerize via hexameric NC1 and dodecameric 7S interactions to form a chicken wire-like network one to several chains thick (Khoshnoodi et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about collagen IV polymerization

claim: The main collagen IV network of the adult GBM consists of collagen α3α4α5(IV) protomers, which are secreted solely by podocytes.
source: The main collagen IV network of the adult GBM consists of collagen α3α4α5(IV) protomers, which are secreted solely by podocytes (Abrahamson et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from previous study on collagen IV expression

claim: Both collagen α3α4α5(IV) NC1 and peri-N epitopes were broadly distributed within the GBM, with positions concentrated close to the center at 12.5 ± 7.2 nm for NC1 and 11.92 ± 3.4 nm for the peri-N epitope.
source: STORM localization of these two disparate epitopes in comparison to agrinC showed that both collagen IV epitopes were broadly distributed within the GBM, with positions concentrated close to the center of the GBM, at 12.5 ± 7.2 nm for NC1 and 11.92 ± 3.4 nm for the peri-N epitope (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Quantitative STORM measurements of collagen IV epitope positions

claim: Collagen α1α1α2(IV) is the major collagen IV isoform in developing glomeruli.
source: In developing glomeruli, collagen α1α1α2(IV) is the major collagen IV isoform.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of glomerular development

claim: In the mature GBM, collagen α1α1α2(IV) is down regulated and mostly replaced by α3α4α5(IV).
source: In the mature GBM, α1α1α2(IV) is down regulated and mostly replaced by α3α4α5(IV) (Miner and Sanes, 1994).
evidence: Cited from previous study on collagen IV isoform expression during development

claim: Collagen α1α1α2(IV) persists at a low level in the adult GBM.
source: However, since α1α1α2(IV) persists at a low level in the adult GBM and is prominent in most other endothelial BMs, we were interested to localize it in relationship to α3α4α5(IV).
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about collagen IV expression

claim: Collagen α1α1α2(IV) localized close to the endothelial side of the GBM with a center position at −59.5 ± 5.2 nm.
source: Collagen α1α1α2(IV) localized close to the endothelial side of the GBM with a center position at −59.5 ± 5.2 nm (Figure 3C), consistent with its known synthesis by endothelial cells (Heidet et al., 2000).
evidence: Quantitative STORM measurements of collagen α1α1α2(IV) position

claim: Collagen α1α1α2(IV) is synthesized by endothelial cells.
source: Collagen α1α1α2(IV) localized close to the endothelial side of the GBM with a center position at −59.5 ± 5.2 nm (Figure 3C), consistent with its known synthesis by endothelial cells (Heidet et al., 2000).
evidence: Cited from previous study on collagen IV synthesis

claim: Collagen α1α1α2(IV) and α3α4α5(IV) showed distinct distributions within the GBM.
source: Importantly, collagen α1α1α2(IV) and α3α4α5(IV) showed distinct distributions within the GBM.
evidence: Comparison of STORM localization data for the two collagen IV isoforms

claim: Nidogen is a 150 kDa dumbbell-shaped glycoprotein that binds to the LEb domain of laminin γ1 and to the collagenous domain of collagen α1α1α2(IV).
source: In all basement membranes, the collagen IV network is thought to be cross-linked to the laminin network by nidogen, a 150 kDa dumbbell-shaped glycoprotein that binds to the LEb domain of laminin γ1 and to the collagenous domain of collagen α1α1α2(IV) (Aumailley et al., 1989).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about nidogen structure and interactions

claim: Nidogen localized to the center of the GBM, with a position of −0.22 ± 3.9 nm.
source: Staining with anti-nidogen localized it to the center of the GBM, with a position of −0.22 ± 3.9 nm, close to both collagen α3α4α5(IV) and LM-521 epitopes (Figure 3D).
evidence: Quantitative STORM measurements of nidogen position

claim: The human GBM is at least two times thicker than the mouse GBM.
source: The human GBM seems to be composed of components that are orthologous to those in mouse, but it is at least two times thicker than the mouse GBM.
evidence: Statement based on known anatomical differences between human and mouse GBM

claim: The peak-to-peak distance of integrin β1 in human GBM was measured to be 428 ± 14.4 nm.
source: The peak-to-peak distance of integrin β1 was measured to be 428 ± 14.4 nm, consistent with the known thickness of the human GBM.
evidence: Quantitative STORM measurements from human kidney sections

claim: In human GBM, the anti-LMα5-LG epitope labeled two layers close to the endothelial and podocyte sides in a location near the integrin β1 epitope.
source: We observed that the anti-LMα5-LG epitope labeled two layers close to the endothelial and podocyte sides of the GBM in a location near the integrin β1 epitope (Figure 5C).
evidence: STORM imaging data from human kidney sections

claim: In human GBM, LMα5-LG was also observed towards the central aspect of the GBM, unlike in mouse.
source: However, unlike the mouse, where LMα5-LG was restricted to the two sides of the GBM, in human we also observed LMα5-LG towards the central aspect of the GBM.
evidence: Comparison of STORM data between human and mouse GBM

claim: Both collagen α3α4α5(IV) NC1 and peri-N epitopes were localized at the center of the human GBM, with a clear separation from integrin β1.
source: Both collagen α3α4α5(IV) epitopes were localized at the center of the GBM, with a clear separation from integrin β1.
evidence: STORM imaging data from human kidney sections

claim: Collagen α1α1α2(IV) was localized to the endothelial side of the human GBM.
source: Staining for collagen α1α1α2(IV) using an antibody to the N-terminal part of the collagenous domain (Foellmer et al., 1983) showed that it was localized to the endothelial side of the GBM (Figure 5D), consistent with previous results using conventional immunofluorescence microscopy (Butkowski et al., 1989).
evidence: STORM imaging data from human kidney sections, consistent with previous immunofluorescence studies

claim: In human GBM, the α1α1α2(IV) network occupies the space between the central α3α4α5(IV) layer and the endothelial surface of the GBM.
source: Further, co-labeling for α3α4α5(IV)-NC1 and α1α1α2(IV) epitopes showed that the two collagen networks had distinct adjacent distributions (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), with the α1α1α2(IV) network occupying the space between the central α3α4α5(IV) layer and the endothelial surface of the GBM.
evidence: STORM co-labeling data from human kidney sections

claim: The increased thickness of the human GBM can be attributed to an expanded collagen α3α4α5(IV) network that is significantly wider than that in the mouse GBM together with an additional layer of LM-521.
source: These data indicate that the increased thickness of the human GBM can be attributed to an expanded collagen α3α4α5(IV) network that is significantly wider than that in the mouse GBM together with an additional layer of LM-521.
evidence: Inference from comparative STORM data between human and mouse GBM

claim: The lack of collagen α3α4α5(IV) network in Col4a3 null mice results in a compensatory increase in the expression of collagen α1α1α2(IV).
source: In both humans and mice, the lack of this network results in a compensatory increase in the expression of collagen α1α1α2(IV), which is normally found at low levels in adult GBM (Kashtan and Kim, 1992; Miner and Sanes, 1996).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on Alport syndrome mouse models

claim: In Alport syndrome, the GBM becomes segmentally split and thickened, associated with hematuria, proteinuria, and progressive renal failure.
source: Despite this compensation, the GBM becomes segmentally split and thickened, and this is associated with hematuria, proteinuria, and progressive renal failure (Hudson et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about Alport syndrome pathology

claim: In the Alport GBM, the two layered organization of agrinC was disrupted in some segments while intact in others.
source: In contrast to the wild-type GBM, the Alport GBM showed segments of capillary loops where the two layered organization of agrinC was disrupted, while in some segments it was intact (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: STORM imaging data from Col4a3 knockout mouse kidney sections

claim: In the Alport GBM, collagen α1α1α2(IV) distribution was spread across the width of the GBM and no longer restricted to the endothelial side.
source: The localization of collagen α1α1α2(IV) was also altered, with its distribution spread across the width of the GBM and no longer restricted to the endothelial side.
evidence: STORM imaging data from Col4a3 knockout mouse kidney sections

claim: Altered collagen α1α1α2(IV) distribution was evident even in capillary loop segments that showed a relatively preserved agrinC organization.
source: This altered collagen α1α1α2(IV) distribution was evident even in capillary loop segments that showed a relatively preserved agrinC organization (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: STORM imaging data from Col4a3 knockout mouse kidney sections

claim: An intact collagen α3α4α5(IV) network helps to maintain agrin and collagen α1α1α2(IV) organization in the healthy GBM.
source: Thus, we conclude that an intact collagen α3α4α5(IV) network helps to maintain agrin and collagen α1α1α2(IV) organization in the healthy GBM.
evidence: Inference from comparison of STORM data between wild-type and Col4a3 knockout mice

claim: The GBM is composed of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins secreted by the endothelial cells and podocytes that flank it.
source: the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), which is composed of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins secreted by the endothelial cells and podocytes that flank it (Miner, 2011).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about GBM composition

claim: The GBM contains specific isoforms of laminin (laminin α5β2γ1, or LM-521), type IV collagen (primarily the collagen α3α4α5(IV) network), heparan sulfate proteoglycan (primarily agrin), and nidogen.
source: The GBM contains specific isoforms of laminin (laminin α5β2γ1, or LM-521), type IV collagen (primarily the collagen α3α4α5(IV) network), heparan sulfate proteoglycan (HSPG) (primarily agrin), and nidogen (Miner, 2012).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about GBM composition

claim: Laminin and type IV collagen self-polymerize into networks that are connected to each other and/or to cell surface receptors by HSPGs and nidogen.
source: Laminin and type IV collagen self-polymerize into networks that are connected to each other and/or to cell surface receptors by HSPGs and nidogen; in addition, some receptors can bind directly to laminin or type IV collagen (Yurchenco et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about ECM protein interactions

claim: Some receptors can bind directly to laminin or type IV collagen.
source: Laminin and type IV collagen self-polymerize into networks that are connected to each other and/or to cell surface receptors by HSPGs and nidogen; in addition, some receptors can bind directly to laminin or type IV collagen (Yurchenco et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about ECM-receptor interactions

claim: The ∼200-nm thickness of a typical mouse GBM is close to the diffraction limited resolution of conventional light microscopy.
source: Second, the ∼200-nm thickness of a typical mouse GBM is close to the diffraction limited resolution of conventional light microscopy, thus preventing its use to analyze GBM ultrastructural and macromolecular organization.
evidence: Statement based on known dimensions of mouse GBM and optical resolution limits

claim: Agrin is a ∼200 kDa protein that is the major HSPG component of the GBM.
source: We began with studies of agrin, a ∼200 kDa protein that is the major HSPG component of the GBM (Groffen et al., 1998).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about agrin

claim: Agrin's N-terminus binds to laminin via the laminin γ1 chain's coiled-coil domain.
source: Agrin's N-terminus (agrinN) binds to laminin via the laminin γ1 chain's coiled-coil domain (Kammerer et al., 1999), whereas agrin's C-terminus (agrinC) binds to integrins and dystroglycan (Singhal and Martin, 2011), receptors present on both podocytes and endothelial cells.
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about agrin-laminin interactions

claim: Agrin's C-terminus binds to integrins and dystroglycan, receptors present on both podocytes and endothelial cells.
source: Agrin's N-terminus (agrinN) binds to laminin via the laminin γ1 chain's coiled-coil domain (Kammerer et al., 1999), whereas agrin's C-terminus (agrinC) binds to integrins and dystroglycan (Singhal and Martin, 2011), receptors present on both podocytes and endothelial cells.
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about agrin-receptor interactions

claim: Integrin β1 is the major integrin β subunit expressed by both podocytes and endothelial cells.
source: We next investigated the position of integrin β1, the major integrin β subunit expressed by both podocytes and endothelial cells (Kreidberg and Symons, 2000).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about integrin expression

claim: Integrin β1 interacts with agrinC.
source: Integrin β1 interacts with agrinC (Martin and Sanes, 1997) (and with laminin; see below).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about integrin-agrin interactions

claim: LM-521 is a cross-shaped heterotrimer that polymerizes in the ECM via interactions among the N-terminal (LN) domains of the α5, β2, and γ1 chains found at the ends of the short arms.
source: LM-521 is a cross-shaped heterotrimer that polymerizes in the ECM via interactions among the N-terminal (LN) domains of the α5, β2, and γ1 chains found at the ends of the short arms (McKee et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about laminin structure and polymerization

claim: LM-521 binds to cell surface receptors, such as integrin α3β1, via the laminin globular (LG) domain of the α5 chain.
source: LM-521 binds to cell surface receptors, such as integrin α3β1, via the laminin globular (LG) domain of the α5 chain (Ido et al., 2004) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about laminin-integrin interactions

claim: Endogenous laminin α5 has been shown to be synthesized by both podocytes and endothelial cells.
source: As endogenous laminin α5 has been shown to be synthesized by both cell types (St John and Abrahamson, 2001), this is a physiologically relevant approach.
evidence: Cited from previous study on laminin α5 expression

claim: The ECM within the GBM is a highly structured and laminated amalgam of interacting protein networks.
source: The results from our study demonstrated that the ECM within the GBM, far from being amorphous, is a highly structured and laminated amalgam of interacting protein networks (Figure 4).
evidence: Summary inference from all STORM data presented in the study

claim: The collagen α3α4α5(IV) N- and C-terminal domains map to near the center of the GBM.
source: One of our most important and unexpected findings was the mapping of the collagen α3α4α5(IV) N- and C-terminal domains to near the center of the GBM, a position that in human GBM is too distant from the positions of the integrin β1 extracellular domain (extending from both podocytes and endothelial cells) for a meaningful ligand–receptor interaction.
evidence: STORM data showing collagen IV positions relative to integrin β1

claim: In human GBM, collagen α3α4α5(IV) is too distant from integrin β1 for a meaningful ligand-receptor interaction.
source: One of our most important and unexpected findings was the mapping of the collagen α3α4α5(IV) N- and C-terminal domains to near the center of the GBM, a position that in human GBM is too distant from the positions of the integrin β1 extracellular domain (extending from both podocytes and endothelial cells) for a meaningful ligand–receptor interaction.
evidence: Inference from STORM measurements of spatial separation between collagen IV and integrin β1

claim: Both agrinC and LMα5LG are the likely biologically relevant ligands for integrin β1 in the GBM.
source: In contrast, both agrinC and LMα5LG localized near integrin β1, implicating them as the likely biologically relevant ligands.
evidence: Inference from STORM data showing spatial proximity of agrinC and LMα5LG to integrin β1

claim: At the endothelial aspect of the GBM, collagen α1α1α2(IV) was near enough to the cell to be capable of binding integrin β1.
source: At the endothelial aspect of the GBM, collagen α1α1α2(IV) was near enough to the cell to be capable of binding integrin β1.
evidence: Inference from STORM measurements showing proximity of collagen α1α1α2(IV) to integrin β1 at endothelial side

claim: In Alport syndrome mouse model, podocytes are exposed to unfamiliar collagen IV ligands due to increased collagen α1α1α2(IV) throughout the GBM.
source: In our Alport syndrome mouse model, which lacks the collagen α3α4α5(IV) network, collagen α1α1α2(IV) was found at increased levels throughout the width of the GBM. One implication of this is that podocytes should be exposed to unfamiliar collagen IV ligands, which might then lead to podocyte injury and the glomerulosclerosis that is observed in the disease.
evidence: Speculation based on STORM data from Alport mouse model

claim: Exposure to unfamiliar collagen IV ligands might lead to podocyte injury and glomerulosclerosis in Alport syndrome.
source: In our Alport syndrome mouse model, which lacks the collagen α3α4α5(IV) network, collagen α1α1α2(IV) was found at increased levels throughout the width of the GBM. One implication of this is that podocytes should be exposed to unfamiliar collagen IV ligands, which might then lead to podocyte injury and the glomerulosclerosis that is observed in the disease.
evidence: Speculation about disease mechanism based on STORM findings

claim: Secreted collagen α3α4α5(IV) protomers are able to permeate through the LM-521 and agrin networks adjacent to the podocyte to reach the center of the GBM.
source: The GBM's collagen α3α4α5(IV) is secreted solely by podocytes (Abrahamson et al., 2009), and our results show that it eventually becomes concentrated near the center of the GBM, away from the podocytes. The secreted collagen α3α4α5(IV) protomers are thus likely able to permeate through the LM-521 and agrin networks adjacent to the podocyte, against the flow of filtrate, to reach the center of the GBM.
evidence: Inference from STORM data showing collagen IV position relative to its site of synthesis

claim: In human glomeruli, the process of collagen α3α4α5(IV) reaching the GBM center should either be faster or persist for a longer period compared to mouse.
source: Given the greater thickness of the human vs the mouse GBM, this process should either be faster or persist for a longer period in human glomeruli.
evidence: Speculation based on comparison of human and mouse GBM thickness

claim: The collagen α1α1α2(IV) protomers made by endothelial cells form a network closely juxtaposed to the endothelium.
source: In contrast, the collagen α1α1α2(IV) protomers made by endothelial cells form a network closely juxtaposed to the endothelium.
evidence: Inference from STORM data showing collagen α1α1α2(IV) position near endothelial side

claim: Different collagen IV protomer behaviors may be fundamental to establishing and maintaining the GBM and could be related to its splitting and thickening in Alport syndrome.
source: These different collagen IV protomer behaviors may be fundamental to establishing and maintaining the GBM and could be related to its splitting and thickening in the setting of Alport syndrome.
evidence: Speculation about GBM maintenance and disease mechanisms based on STORM findings

claim: A modification of the Tokuyasu method of cryo-embedding and cryosectioning at 200 nanometers thickness was optimal for STORM imaging of kidney sections.
source: These preliminary studies established that a modification of the Tokuyasu method of cryo-embedding and cryosectioning at 200 nanometers (nm) thickness was optimal (Tokuyasu, 1973).
evidence: Empirical optimization of tissue preparation methods for STORM

claim: Podocalyxin is expressed on the surfaces of both endothelial cells and podocytes.
source: We next imaged the relationship between the GBM and the flanking podocytes and endothelial cells by double labeling with antibodies to agrinC and to the sialoprotein podocalyxin, which is expressed on the surfaces of both endothelial cells and podocytes (Kerjaschki et al., 1984).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about podocalyxin expression
